newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Rate cuts, bank closures no panacea for Bulgaria.
newsitem.headline: Rate cuts, bank closures no panacea for Bulgaria.

text.p: Rate cuts and bank closures are the only tools left to Bulgaria's central bank to stabilise the crumbling economy but analysts say their healing effect may be shortlived as they boost inflation.

Bulgaria's central bank, moving to clean up its crumbling banking system at the start of an International Monetary Fund mission, on Thursday began bankruptcy proceedings for eight of nine banks placed in receivership in September.
"What we actually need is more economic activity. In a weak economy like this there is not enough business to go round the banks," head of Raiffeisenbank Bulgaria Douglas Dryden told Reuters.
"In such a small economy they are doomed to failure."
The central bank also cut the annual interest rate to 180 percent on Thursday as part of attempts to boost investment and lay the ground for next year's budget frame.
Rates were temporarily hiked to a record 300 percent in September in a bid to stabilise the shaken financial system and are gradually being reduced.

"Both the rate cut and bank closures aimed to restore confidence in banks and the lev...The question is how lasting they are going to be," chief economist of the Bulgarian Investment Bank Galina Dimitrova told Reuters.
"So far the rate hike succeded in containing money supply and curbed inflation," she added.
The rate cut boosts pressure on the lev and inflation and it is difficult to predict what will happen after yet another slump of the lev on the local interbank market, said Dimitrova.
The lev slid from 70 per dollar in January to 244 on Friday. The lev eased from 242 on Thursday after the rate cut.

If opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov wins Sunday's second round of presidential elections, as opinion polls predict, the defeat of the governing Socialists could spark a cabinet reshuffle and the upheaval could delay economic reforms again.
The government postponed approval of next year's budget frame by two months until December due to uncertain macroeconomic parameters like interest rate, inflation and lev/dollar exchange rate.

"I don't believe in the quick stabilisation of the banking sector. I do not know what inflation will be next month, nor how much the dollar will be (against the lev) next week," wrote Evgeni Petrov, editor of Pari business daily.
"Making a business plan under these conditions is like chasing a black cat in a dark room," he added.

If the IMF approves Bulgaria's reform performance, the debt -ridden country stands to get a $115 million loan, which would provide a breath of air, but would not solve the country's payments problems.
If the IMF once again delays funding, the chances of Bulgaria defaulting on foreign debt payments will rise.
If the financial system fails to stabilise in the short term, the next logical step would be to curb operations of the central bank and replace it with a foreign currency board.

Critics of the currency board say that the size of Bulgaria's unofficial or so-called grey economy is so big that the currency board will either be ineffective or all private business, mostly operating in the grey, will be stifled.

In a bid to boost tax revenue the socialist government, in power since January, has imposed draconian taxes on small businesses, while generously subsidising loss-making state industries. Tax evasion is the only way for private businesses to keep afloat.
Hoping to win IMF funding, the government agreed in July to close 64 loss-makers out of 2,000.
"If there is very strong political will to retain a command economy it will not work in the long term here and recovery will be delayed," said Dryden.
